findings.title: Diesel Dominates Fuel Type, But Petrol Accounts for the Volume of Budget Cars
findings.question: Which fuel type is most common?
findings.finding_summary: Diesel is the most common fuel type (54.5% of 6,717 vehicles) and commands a 64% higher median resale price than petrol cars (Rs.5.25L vs Rs.3.20L). CNG and LPG combined account for only 1.3% of listings.
findings.limitation: Listing proportions reflect seller behaviour rather than the nationwide on-road vehicle distribution.

findings.title: Selling Price Is Strongly Right-Skewed: Most Cars Are Affordable But a Luxury Tail Inflates the Average
findings.question: How is the selling price distributed?
findings.finding_summary: The median price of Rs.4.2L is the best measure of a typical used car. The mean (Rs.5.26L) is inflated by 306 high-end outliers (up to Rs.1 Crore). 98.4% of cars are priced below Rs.20 Lakh.
findings.limitation: Outliers were retained as genuine luxury vehicles; removing them would not reflect the full market.

findings.title: Newer Vehicles Command Higher Prices: Approximately Rs.57,000 More Per Year of Manufacturing
findings.question: Is vehicle manufacturing year associated with selling price?
findings.finding_summary: Manufacturing year has a moderate positive association with price (r=+0.427, p<0.0001). Each newer year is associated with approximately Rs.57,405 more in price. The 2020 dip reflects very few listings (n=63) and a shift to BS6-petrol vehicles.
findings.limitation: Year alone explains only 18.3% of price variance (R-squared=0.183). Vehicle condition and service history are unavailable.

findings.title: Automatic Transmission Cars Carry a 112.5% Median Price Premium Over Manual Cars
findings.question: Do manual and automatic cars show different price distributions?
findings.finding_summary: Automatic cars (8.6% of listings) have a median price more than double that of manual cars (Rs.8.5L vs Rs.4.0L). This gap is partly driven by automatic cars having bigger engines and more power, not the gearbox alone.
findings.limitation: Transmission type is confounded with vehicle segment and brand; causal separation is not possible with this dataset.

findings.title: Ownership History Is Associated With Depreciation: 36% Price Drop from First to Second Owner
findings.question: Additional finding on ownership and depreciation.
findings.finding_summary: Each ownership transfer is associated with a significant price reduction. First to second owner sees the steepest drop of 36% (Rs.5.0L to Rs.3.2L). By the fourth-or-more owner stage, median price falls to Rs.1.85L.
findings.limitation: Ownership history cannot distinguish between cars that changed hands due to upgrades versus mechanical problems.

findings.title: Engine Power Is the Strongest Single Numerical Predictor of Resale Price (r = +0.692)
findings.question: Which numerical features show stronger correlations?
findings.finding_summary: Max Power (bhp) is the strongest numerical predictor of selling price (r=+0.692). Engine CC, Torque, and Year also show positive associations. Mileage (kmpl) has a strong negative association with engine size (r=-0.593), confirming the classic power-efficiency trade-off.
findings.limitation: Pearson r measures linear association only. Non-linear effects and categorical confounders are not captured.

findings.title: German Luxury Brands Command Median Prices 7-8x Higher Than Budget Brands
findings.question: Which brands have higher average selling prices?
findings.finding_summary: BMW (Rs.25L), Audi (Rs.20L) and Mercedes-Benz (Rs.18.9L) lead on median price. Maruti (Rs.3.5L) dominates by volume (31.1% share). Maruti and Hyundai together hold ~50% of the market. Only 17 brands had >= 30 listings; smaller brands excluded to avoid small-sample bias.
findings.limitation: Brand median prices are influenced by the model mix listed — a brand appearing only in entry-level models will show a lower median regardless of its true capabilities.

findings.title: Kilometres Driven Has Only a Weak Association With Price; Decline Is Clearest in Early Usage Buckets
findings.question: Is kilometres driven associated with selling price?
findings.finding_summary: KM driven has a weak but statistically significant negative association with price (r=-0.161). Median price drops from Rs.5.7L (< 30k km) to Rs.3.25L (150-200k km). The > 200k km bucket shows a price uptick, likely due to durable diesel fleet vehicles. Max KM recorded: 2.36 million (a commercial Hyundai).
findings.limitation: KM alone is a poor price predictor compared to engine power and vehicle age. Actual mechanical condition data is unavailable.
